questions.prompt: What do OSPF routers flood so that they all build the same map of the network?

options.text: Their full routing tables, sent to every neighbor every 30 seconds
Link-state advertisements (LSAs) that describe their links
Their ARP caches and MAC address tables

questions.explanation: LSAs describe each router's links. Flooded through the area, they give every router the same link-state database to run SPF on.

questions.prompt: Which statement enables OSPF area 0 on the interface 192.168.5.1/24 and on nothing else?
questions.explanation: A 0.0.0.0 wildcard matches exactly one address. The /16 wildcard would also enable every other 192.168.x.x interface, and the last option uses the wrong area.

questions.prompt: Two routers on one /30 link show no OSPF neighbors, although their areas match. Which of these must also match?

options.text: Their hostnames, which OSPF exchanges in every hello packet
Their OSPF process IDs, the number after `router ospf`
Subnet and mask, plus timers and authentication on real routers

questions.explanation: Process IDs are local to each router and hostnames play no part. Neighbors must agree on the subnet, the mask and the hello parameters.

questions.prompt: What do the numbers in `O 10.3.3.0/24 [110/3] via 10.0.12.2` mean?

options.text: Administrative distance 110 and OSPF cost 3
Process 110 and area 3
Learned 110 seconds ago, 3 hops away

questions.explanation: The first number ranks the route source (OSPF is 110 by default) and the second is the total cost to the destination.

questions.prompt: Why make a LAN interface passive in OSPF?

options.text: To stop advertising the LAN's subnet to the other OSPF routers
To advertise the subnet but send no hellos and form no adjacency
To shut the interface down while OSPF is still converging

questions.explanation: Passive interfaces stay in OSPF, so their subnet is still advertised, but no neighbor can form there. That also blocks rogue adjacencies from the LAN.

courses.title: 8. DHCP and DNS services
courses.summary: Hand out addresses automatically with DHCP and turn names into addresses with DNS. Follow the DORA exchange, build router DHCP pools with excluded ranges, read DNS records with nslookup, and open an intranet page by name. The lab takes a branch office from no addresses to a working web page.

lessons.title: DHCP and the DORA exchange
paragraphs: The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP, RFC 2131) gives hosts their IP settings automatically: address, mask, default gateway and DNS server, together with a lease time. Clients use UDP port 68 and servers UDP port 67. Without DHCP every laptop would need hand-typed settings, and mistakes such as duplicate addresses would be common.

A client with no address talks in four steps, called DORA. It broadcasts a Discover from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255. A server answers with an Offer, the client broadcasts a Request for that offer, and the server confirms with an Acknowledge. The client then uses the address until the lease ends; real clients renew halfway through the lease, while the lab has no lease timers.

Routers do not forward broadcasts, so a Discover never leaves its subnet. Real networks run a DHCP relay on the router (`ip helper-address` in the widely used router CLI style) to pass requests to a central server. The VoltQuest lab does not simulate relays, so the router must hold a pool for each subnet it serves directly. When no server answers, the lab prints `DHCP request failed.`, while Windows would fall back to a 169.254.x.x link-local address.
lessons.example:
! Ask any DHCP server on this subnet for a lease
C:\> ipconfig /renew
! Show the lease: address, mask, gateway and DNS server
C:\> ipconfig /all
! Give the address back, then ask again
C:\> ipconfig /release
C:\> ipconfig /renew
lessons.pitfall: Expecting DHCP to cross a router by itself. The Discover is a broadcast, and routers stop broadcasts. A client in a subnet without a local pool or a relay never gets an offer.

question.prompt: In which order do the four DHCP messages travel?

options.text: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
Request, Offer, Discover, Acknowledge
Offer, Discover, Acknowledge, Request

question.explanation: The client discovers servers, a server offers an address, the client requests that offer, and the server acknowledges it: DORA.

lessons.title: A router as DHCP server
paragraphs: A router can serve DHCP itself. First exclude the addresses you assign by hand, in global configuration: `ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.20`. Then create a pool with `ip dhcp pool STAFF`, which opens the `(dhcp-config)#` prompt, and set `network`, `default-router` and `dns-server`.

The lab's router answers a Discover from the pool whose network and mask match the interface that received it, and leases the lowest free address that is neither excluded nor its own. Real servers may choose differently, and many first ping an address to check that nobody uses it, so never rely on a particular number: give servers and printers static addresses outside the pool, or reservations.

`show ip dhcp binding` lists every leased address with the client's MAC address. On the client, `ipconfig /all` shows `DHCP Enabled: Yes` together with the leased address, gateway and DNS server. Real pools also set a lease time and a domain name; the lab's pools take the network, the gateway and the DNS server only.
lessons.example:
R1> enable
R1# configure terminal
! Keep the gateway and the fixed servers out of the pool
R1(config)# ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.20
R1(config)# ip dhcp pool STAFF
R1(dhcp-config)# network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
R1(dhcp-config)# default-router 192.168.10.1
R1(dhcp-config)# dns-server 192.168.10.5
R1(dhcp-config)# end
R1# show ip dhcp binding
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting the exclusions. Without `ip dhcp excluded-address`, the pool can lease a PC the address that a server or printer already uses. The lab's DHCP server does no conflict check at all, so the duplicate appears at once.

question.prompt: Where do you type `ip dhcp excluded-address`?

options.text: Inside the DHCP pool, at the `(dhcp-config)#` prompt
In global configuration, at the `(config)#` prompt
In interface configuration mode

question.explanation: Exclusions apply to every pool on the router, so they live in global configuration.

lessons.title: DNS: names to addresses
paragraphs: The Domain Name System (DNS, RFC 1034 and RFC 1035) maps names to addresses. A host's resolver sends a query, usually over UDP port 53, to its configured DNS server, which answers from its own records or asks other servers on the client's behalf. Answers are cached for their time to live, so repeated lookups are fast.

Records have types. An A record maps a name to an IPv4 address and an AAAA record to an IPv6 address. A CNAME makes one name an alias of another, MX names a domain's mail servers, NS names its DNS servers and PTR maps an address back to a name. The lab's DNS service stores A records only.

`nslookup <name>` shows which server answered and the address it returned; a name the server does not know gives `Non-existent domain`. If no answer arrives, the resolver retries; after three lost queries the lab prints `DNS request timed out.`, which points at reachability, not at a missing record. In labs, use names under a reserved domain such as `.test` (RFC 6761), so they never collide with real ones. DNS answers can be forged; DNSSEC adds signatures, which the lab does not simulate.
lessons.example:
! Which DNS server does this PC use?
C:\> ipconfig /all
! Ask that server for the A record of a name
C:\> nslookup intranet.voltquest.test
! Use the name directly: the PC resolves it first
C:\> ping intranet.voltquest.test
lessons.pitfall: Blaming DNS for a routing fault, or the reverse. Ping the server's IP address first. If the address works but the name fails, check the DNS server setting and the records; if the address fails too, fix addressing or routing before you touch DNS.

question.prompt: `ping 192.168.10.5` works, but `ping intranet.voltquest.test` cannot find the host. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A missing route between the PC and 192.168.10.5
A shut switch port on the server's LAN
A wrong DNS server setting or a missing DNS record

question.explanation: The successful ping by address proves the path. Only name resolution is left, so check the client's DNS server and the record on that server.

lessons.title: Browsing by name, end to end
paragraphs: Opening http://intranet.voltquest.test chains several services. The PC needs a lease (DHCP), the MAC address of the next hop (ARP), the server's address (DNS), a TCP connection to port 80, and finally the HTTP request and response. Each step depends on the ones before it, so troubleshoot in the same order.

TCP (RFC 9293) sets up a connection before data flows. Real TCP uses a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN+ACK, ACK), acknowledges data and closes with FIN segments. The lab simplifies a web request to four segments: SYN, SYN+ACK, the request and the response. HTTP (RFC 9110) then carries `GET /` and a status such as 200 OK. Plain HTTP on TCP port 80 is unencrypted; real sites use HTTPS on TCP port 443.

Ping and the browser test different things. A ping reply proves that the host is reachable at layer 3; it says nothing about the web service. If the server's web service is off, ping still works while the browser reports `Connection refused: no web service is listening.`, because the server resets the TCP connection.
lessons.example:
1  DHCP  PC1 leases 192.168.10.21, gateway 192.168.10.1, DNS 192.168.10.5
2  ARP   PC1 learns the DNS server's MAC (same subnet, no router needed)
3  DNS   query A intranet.voltquest.test over UDP 53, answer 192.168.10.5
4  TCP   SYN to port 80, then SYN+ACK from the server
5  HTTP  GET / and the reply 200 OK with the page
lessons.pitfall: Testing a web server with ping only. ICMP replies prove the host is up, not that anything listens on TCP port 80. Test the service itself with the browser.

question.prompt: Which transport protocol and port does plain HTTP use by default?

options.text: UDP 53
TCP 443
TCP 80

question.explanation: HTTP runs over TCP port 80. TCP 443 is HTTPS, and UDP 53 is DNS.

steps: Run `ipconfig` on PC1: it is a DHCP client without a lease, so it shows 0.0.0.0. `ipconfig /renew` prints `DHCP request failed.` because no server exists yet.
On R1 exclude the fixed addresses: `ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.10.1 192.168.10.20` and `ip dhcp excluded-address 192.168.20.1 192.168.20.20`.

Create `ip dhcp pool STAFF` with `network 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0`, `default-router 192.168.10.1` and `dns-server 192.168.10.5`. Then create pool LAB for 192.168.20.0/24 with gateway 192.168.20.1 and the same DNS server.

On PC1 run `nslookup intranet.voltquest.test`, then open http://intranet.voltquest.test in the browser.

On PC3 run `nslookup intranet.voltquest.test`, then open http://intranet.voltquest.test. Both cross R1; in the step-by-step view the first query may be dropped while R1 resolves ARP, and the resolver's retry gets through.
Press Check results.
courses.expected: The first lease in each LAN is .21, because .1 to .20 are excluded. `show ip dhcp binding` lists three bindings, `nslookup` answers 192.168.10.5 on PC1 and PC3, and all three PCs open the intranet by name, PC3 across R1.

lab.title: Bring a branch office online with DHCP and DNS

Server1 (192.168.10.5) already runs DNS and the intranet web site, with an A record for intranet.voltquest.test. The PCs are DHCP clients, but no DHCP server exists. PC3 leases an address with gateway 192.168.20.1
PC1 opens the intranet by name
PC2 opens the intranet by name

questions.prompt: Why does a DHCP Discover go to the broadcast address 255.255.255.255?

options.text: The client has no address yet and does not know where a server is
DHCP messages are always broadcasts, even when a client renews
To reach the DNS servers on the Internet at the same time

questions.explanation: A client without an address cannot target a server it does not know, so it asks everyone on the subnet. Later renewals can be unicast.

questions.prompt: A pool covers 192.168.20.0/24, but the router interface facing those clients has 192.168.21.1/24. What happens when a client there sends a Discover?

options.text: The client gets an address from 192.168.20.0/24 anyway, with gateway .1
No offer: the pool must match the subnet of the receiving interface
The router forwards the Discover to the next router

questions.explanation: The server picks the pool by the subnet the request arrived on. With no matching pool, the client gets no offer, and routers do not forward the broadcast.

questions.prompt: Which DNS record type maps a name to an IPv4 address?

options.text: MX
PTR
A

questions.explanation: An A record holds an IPv4 address. MX names mail servers, and PTR maps an address back to a name.

questions.prompt: The browser shows `Connection refused`, but ping to the server works. What does that tell you?

options.text: The host is reachable, but nothing listens on TCP port 80
The DNS record for the server points to the wrong address
The PC's default gateway is missing, so replies cannot return

questions.explanation: The ping proves the path and the address. A refused connection means the server answered the TCP request with a reset because no web service is running.

questions.prompt: Why should servers usually keep static addresses outside the DHCP pool?

options.text: DHCP servers refuse to lease addresses to devices that run services
Clients and DNS records rely on the server's address staying the same
Static addresses make the server's traffic faster than leased ones

questions.explanation: DNS records and client settings point at the server's address. A changing lease would break them, so servers get static addresses or reservations.

courses.title: 9. Access control lists
courses.summary: Filter traffic on a router with access control lists. Read wildcard masks, write standard, extended and named lists, and apply them in the right place and direction. Learn how first match and the implicit deny decide every packet, and use ACLs for least-privilege segmentation: keep guests away from a staff web server while still letting them ping it.

lessons.title: How routers process access lists
paragraphs: An access control list (ACL) is an ordered list of permit and deny entries. When a packet meets an interface that has an ACL, the router compares it with the entries from the top down. The first entry that matches decides the packet's fate, and the router stops reading. If no entry matches, an invisible implicit deny at the end drops the packet.

You apply an ACL to an interface in one direction: inbound, for packets entering the interface (checked before routing), or outbound, for packets leaving it (checked after routing). Each interface holds at most one list per direction. The lab's router drops a denied packet and, like many real routers, tells the sender with an ICMP administratively prohibited message, which the lab's PCs show as `Communication administratively prohibited.`

ACLs are a tool for least privilege: permit only the traffic a group needs and deny the rest. They decide who can reach a service; they do not fix the service. If a web application has a flaw, anyone still allowed to reach it can exploit it, so filtering and fixing the application are both needed. Classic ACLs are also stateless: they judge each packet alone, so replies need their own permit.
lessons.example:
access list GUEST-IN, applied inbound on the guest interface
  10 deny tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq www
  20 permit ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 any
Guest to 192.168.30.10, TCP port 80:  matches 10, denied
Guest to 192.168.30.10, ICMP echo:    skips 10, matches 20, permitted
Guest to 203.0.113.10, TCP port 80:   skips 10, matches 20, permitted
Any packet that matches no entry:     implicit deny, dropped
lessons.pitfall: Forgetting the implicit deny. A list that contains only deny entries blocks every packet on that interface, including the traffic you meant to allow. End the list with an explicit permit for the traffic that should still pass.

question.prompt: A packet matches entry 20, a permit, and would also match entry 30, a deny. What happens?

options.text: It is denied, because deny entries win
It is permitted, because the first matching entry decides
The router counts permits and denies and takes the majority

question.explanation: The router stops at the first match. Entry 30 is never read for this packet, which is why the order of entries matters.

lessons.title: Wildcard masks and standard ACLs
paragraphs: ACL entries match addresses with wildcard masks, just like OSPF network statements: 0 bits must match and 1 bits are ignored. `192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255` matches the whole /24, `host 192.168.10.50` is short for `192.168.10.50 0.0.0.0`, and `any` is short for `0.0.0.0 255.255.255.255`. For a /26 the wildcard is 0.0.0.63, and for a /30 it is 0.0.0.3.

Standard ACLs, numbered 1 to 99 in the lab, match only the source address. `access-list 10 deny 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255` stops packets from that subnet, whatever their destination. Because they cannot tell destinations apart, standard ACLs belong as close to the destination as possible; near the source they would cut the source off from everything.

Add a `remark` line that says why an entry exists. Entries are appended in the order you type them. Real routers also let you insert or delete single entries by sequence number; in the lab, rebuild a list with `no access-list 10` (or `no ip access-list extended NAME` for a named list) when the order is wrong.
lessons.example:
R1> enable
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# access-list 10 remark Staff: only the admin PC may reach the server LAN
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit host 192.168.10.50
R1(config)# access-list 10 deny 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# access-list 10 permit any
R1(config)# interface g0/2
R1(config-if)# ip access-group 10 out
R1(config-if)# end
R1# show access-lists
lessons.pitfall: Using a subnet mask where a wildcard belongs. `access-list 10 deny 192.168.20.0 255.255.255.0` does not mean the /24. The lab rejects that wildcard; real routers accept it and match every address that ends in .0 instead. The /24 wildcard is 0.0.0.255.

question.prompt: Which wildcard matches every host in 10.10.8.0/21?
question.explanation: A /21 mask is 255.255.248.0, and 255.255.255.255 minus that is 0.0.7.255. 255.255.248.0 is the subnet mask itself, not a wildcard.

lessons.title: Extended and named ACLs
paragraphs: Extended ACLs, numbered 100 to 199 in the lab or named, match the protocol, the source, the destination and, for TCP and UDP, the destination port. The order is fixed: `permit|deny <protocol> <source> <destination> [eq <port>]`. Ports may be numbers or names, such as `eq 80` or `eq www` and `eq 53` or `eq domain`. For ICMP the lab accepts the `echo` and `echo-reply` types.

Because they are so precise, extended ACLs belong close to the source: unwanted traffic is dropped before it crosses the network, and nothing else is affected. To block guests from one web server, deny TCP from the guest subnet to that host on port 80, permit the rest, and apply the list inbound on the guest interface.

Named lists are easier to read and maintain. `ip access-list extended GUEST-IN` opens the `(config-ext-nacl)#` prompt, where you type entries without the list name, and `ip access-group GUEST-IN in` applies the list. Real routers can also match source ports, port ranges and established TCP sessions; the lab matches destination ports only.
lessons.example:
R1> enable
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# ip access-list extended GUEST-IN
R1(config-ext-nacl)# remark Guests may not open the staff web server
R1(config-ext-nacl)# deny tcp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq www
R1(config-ext-nacl)# permit ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 any
R1(config-ext-nacl)# exit
R1(config)# interface g0/0.20
R1(config-subif)# ip access-group GUEST-IN in
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show access-lists
lessons.pitfall: Putting the port on the wrong side. A web server listens on destination port 80, and the client's source port is random. Write `eq 80` after the destination. The lab only accepts a port there; real routers also accept one after the source, where it would match the server's replies instead of the requests.

question.prompt: Which single entry blocks the guest subnet 192.168.20.0/24 from the web service on 192.168.30.10 without blocking anything else?
question.explanation: Only that entry names the protocol, the source subnet, the server and the port. The first option blocks all traffic to the server, and the second blocks the guests from every web server. A permit entry must still follow for the traffic that should pass.

lessons.title: Placement, direction and verification
paragraphs: Direction is always seen from the router. Inbound on the guest gateway sees packets that come from the guests; outbound on the same interface sees packets going to the guests. An outbound list does not filter packets that the router itself creates, such as its own pings. Draw the packet's path and ask where, and in which direction, it first meets the router.

Verify with `show access-lists`: each entry shows its sequence number (10, 20, 30 and so on) and how many packets matched it. `clear access-list counters` resets the counts before a test, and `show running-config` shows where each list is applied. Test both sides: what must fail, and what must still work.

An inbound list also filters traffic addressed to the router itself. A DHCP Discover arrives from source 0.0.0.0 to UDP port 67, so any inbound list on an interface with DHCP clients must permit it, for example with `permit udp any any eq bootps` at the top; the lab enforces this too. Real routers filter OSPF hellos the same way, which the lab does not model as packets. Applying a list name that does not exist permits everything, in the lab and in the widely used router CLI style alike.
lessons.example:
R1> enable
! Which entry did each packet hit?
R1# show access-lists
! Start a clean test
R1# clear access-list counters
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface g0/0.20
! Wrong direction: remove it, then apply it inbound
R1(config-subif)# no ip access-group GUEST-IN out
R1(config-subif)# ip access-group GUEST-IN in
R1(config-subif)# end
R1# show running-config

Applied `out` on the guest interface, it only sees packets going to the guests, whose source never matches the permit, so the implicit deny drops every reply and the guests lose all connectivity.

Inbound on the interface that faces the guests, close to the source
Inbound on the router interface that faces the Internet uplink

question.explanation: Inbound on the guest gateway, the list sees every guest packet before it is routed, and it affects nobody else.

Nothing: every other packet hits the implicit deny

options.text: It matches only the source, so near the source it would cut that source off from everything
Standard lists can only be applied outbound, and outbound means near the destination

courses.title: 10. NAT, PAT and a secure branch capstone
courses.summary: Connect private networks to the Internet with NAT. Learn the inside and outside terms, publish a server with static NAT, share one public address with PAT, and read the translation table. Then combine VLANs, DHCP, an access list and NAT in a branch network, and see why NAT is not a security control.

lessons.title: Why NAT exists: inside and outside
paragraphs: IPv4 has about 4.3 billion addresses, far fewer than the devices that want one. Private RFC 1918 ranges let every organization reuse the same addresses internally, but the Internet does not route them. Network address translation (NAT, RFC 3022) rewrites addresses at the border: inside hosts use private addresses, and the router swaps in a public address on the way out and back again on the way in.

NAT has its own vocabulary. Interfaces are inside (`ip nat inside`) or outside (`ip nat outside`). An inside local address is the private address configured on an inside host, and an inside global address is the public address that represents that host outside. Outside global is the real address of a host on the Internet, and outside local is how inside hosts see it, usually the same address.

The router translates only traffic that crosses from an inside interface to an outside interface, or back, and keeps a table of active translations. NAT breaks the end-to-end model: an outside host cannot start a session to an inside host unless a mapping exists. IPv6 has enough addresses for every device and removes the need for NAT; the lab does not simulate IPv6.
lessons.example:
Term            Example          Meaning
Inside local    192.168.10.21    private address on the inside host
Inside global   203.0.113.2      public address that stands for it outside
Outside global  198.51.100.10    real address of the Internet server
Outside local   198.51.100.10    how inside hosts see that server (the same here)
lessons.pitfall: Marking interfaces backwards. If the LAN interface is `ip nat outside` and the provider link `ip nat inside`, LAN traffic leaves untranslated with private source addresses, and the replies never come back.

question.prompt: In NAT terms, what is the inside global address?

options.text: The private address configured on the inside host's network card
The public address that represents an inside host to the outside
The address of the provider's DNS server, as seen from the inside

question.explanation: Inside describes whose address it is, and global says where it is used. The inside global address is what the Internet sees for the inside host.

lessons.title: Static NAT for a server
paragraphs: Static NAT maps one inside local address to one inside global address, permanently and in both directions: `ip nat inside source static 192.168.30.10 203.0.113.10`. Packets from the server leave with source 203.0.113.10, and packets that arrive for 203.0.113.10 are delivered to 192.168.30.10. That is how you publish an internal server to the Internet.

The public address must reach your router. It can come from the outside interface's own subnet, and then the router answers ARP for it on that interface, or from a separate block that the provider routes to your router. In this course the provider routes 203.0.113.8/29 to the branch router, because the /30 link has no spare address, and the server uses 203.0.113.10 from it.

A one-to-one mapping forwards every protocol and every port, not just the web service. Publishing a server with static NAT therefore exposes all of it. Real designs forward only the ports they need (static PAT, often called port forwarding) and add filtering on the outside interface or a stateful firewall; the lab supports one-to-one static NAT only. Filters on the outside interface see public addresses: an inbound list runs before arriving packets are translated, and an outbound list runs after leaving packets are translated.
lessons.example:
R1> enable
R1# configure terminal
R1(config)# interface g0/0
R1(config-if)# ip nat inside
R1(config-if)# interface g0/1
R1(config-if)# ip nat outside
R1(config-if)# exit
! Publish the web server: one inside address, one public address
R1(config)# ip nat inside source static 192.168.30.10 203.0.113.10
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip nat translations
lessons.pitfall: Thinking static NAT publishes only the web service. A one-to-one mapping forwards every protocol to the server, so anything it answers, from ping to remote administration, is reachable from the Internet until you filter it.

question.prompt: What does `ip nat inside source static 192.168.30.10 203.0.113.10` do?

options.text: Maps the server to 203.0.113.10 for good, so outside hosts can start connections
Translates the server only while the server itself has a session open to the outside
Publishes only TCP port 80 of the server and blocks every other port and protocol

question.explanation: A static entry always exists, so traffic for 203.0.113.10 is translated whoever starts it. NAT itself filters nothing.

lessons.title: PAT: many hosts behind one address
paragraphs: Port address translation (PAT), also called NAT overload, lets many inside hosts share one public address. The router rewrites each session's source port (for ICMP, the query ID) as well as the address, and records the mapping in its translation table. Replies come back to the shared address and port, and the table tells the router which inside host and port to restore.

Configure PAT with an access list that selects which inside sources to translate, and one command that ties it to the outside interface: `ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload`. Here the access list classifies traffic for NAT; it filters nothing. `show ip nat translations` lists each entry with its protocol and the inside global, inside local, outside local and outside global addresses and ports.

When two inside hosts use the same source port or ICMP ID, the router gives one of them a different port on the outside, so the replies stay apart; in the lab, the second host's ICMP ID 1 becomes 1024. PAT also stops outside hosts from starting sessions to inside hosts, but treat that as a side effect, not as a security policy.
lessons.example:
R1> enable
R1# configure terminal
! Which inside sources may be translated
R1(config)# access-list 1 permit 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255
R1(config)# access-list 1 permit 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255
! Share the address of g0/1 among all of them
R1(config)# ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload
R1(config)# end
R1# show ip nat translations
R1# clear ip nat translation *
lessons.pitfall: A NAT access list that misses a subnet. If `access-list 1` permits 192.168.10.0/24 only, hosts in 192.168.20.0/24 leave with their private addresses, and the provider cannot route the replies back.

question.prompt: How does PAT tell apart two inside hosts that share the public address 203.0.113.2?

options.text: By their MAC addresses, which the router keeps per session
By the TTL value each host puts in its packets
By a unique port or ICMP ID per session in the translation table

question.explanation: The translation table maps each public address and port pair back to one inside address and port. MAC addresses never leave the LAN, and the TTL changes at every hop.

lessons.title: Capstone design: a secure branch
paragraphs: A small branch combines everything in this track. VLANs separate staff, guests and servers. A router-on-a-stick gives each VLAN its gateway. DHCP pools hand out addresses with the right gateway and DNS server. An access list limits what guests can reach. NAT connects the private ranges to the Internet: PAT for the users and static NAT for the published server.

Segmentation is what limits damage. If a guest laptop is infected, the guest ACL keeps it away from staff PCs and the servers; if the published web server is compromised, filtering between VLANs limits where an attacker can go next. NAT does none of this: it changes addresses, and static NAT exposes the server completely. Real edges also run a stateful firewall, and real devices need passwords, SSH and logging, which this lab does not model.

Verify a design layer by layer and keep the evidence: leases (`ipconfig /all`, `show ip dhcp binding`), routing (`show ip route`, `tracert`), filtering (`show access-lists` counters, one blocked and one allowed test) and translation (`show ip nat translations`). In the lab, a first ping that crosses two routers can lose two echoes to ARP before the replies arrive.
lessons.example:
Area         Branch design decision
VLANs        10 STAFF, 20 GUEST, 30 SERVERS on S1, trunk to R1
Gateways     R1 g0/0.10, g0/0.20 and g0/0.30, each .1 in its subnet
DHCP         pools STAFF and GUEST on R1, .1 to .20 excluded
Filtering    GUEST-IN inbound on g0/0.20: DHCP and DNS only inside, Internet allowed
NAT          PAT on g0/1 for STAFF and GUEST, static 192.168.30.10 as 203.0.113.10
Routing      default route to the provider at 203.0.113.1
lessons.pitfall: Treating NAT as a firewall. Static NAT forwards every protocol to the published server, and PAT blocks unsolicited inbound traffic only as a side effect. Write explicit filtering rules for every segment and for the Internet edge.

question.prompt: Which statement about NAT and security is accurate?

options.text: NAT only changes addresses; filtering must come from access lists or a firewall
PAT encrypts the traffic it translates, so it works like a VPN for the users
Static NAT forwards only web traffic, which keeps the published server safe

question.explanation: NAT rewrites addresses and ports. It neither encrypts nor filters, and a static mapping forwards every protocol.

steps: Check the starting point: `show vlan brief` and `show interfaces trunk` on S1, `show ip interface brief` on R1. The VLANs, trunk and gateways work, but PC1 and PC2 have no addresses and R1 has no route to the Internet.
DHCP: on R1 exclude .1 to .20 in 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24, create pools STAFF and GUEST with gateway .1 and DNS server 192.168.30.10, then run `ipconfig /renew` on PC1 and PC2.

Guest filter: `ip access-list extended GUEST-IN` with `permit udp any any eq bootps`, `permit udp 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 host 192.168.30.10 eq domain`, `deny ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 192.168.0.0 0.0.255.255` and `permit ip 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255 any`. Apply it with `ip access-group GUEST-IN in` on g0/0.20. Keep the first entry: a DHCP Discover comes from 0.0.0.0, so without it the implicit deny blocks guest leases. Run `ipconfig /renew` on PC2 again to prove it still gets one.

NAT: mark g0/0.10, g0/0.20 and g0/0.30 `ip nat inside` and g0/1 `ip nat outside`. Add `access-list 1` entries for 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.20.0/24, then `ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/1 overload` and `ip nat inside source static 192.168.30.10 203.0.113.10`.
Add `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 203.0.113.1`. Ping 198.51.100.10 from PC1 and PC2 (the first echoes can be lost to ARP at R1 and R2), then read `show ip nat translations`.
From PC3, the Internet user, ping 203.0.113.10. Static NAT delivers it to Server1, which proves that the server now answers the Internet on every protocol, not only on port 80.

Test the guest limits: on PC2, `nslookup www.branch.test` works because GUEST-IN permits DNS, but http://192.168.30.10 and a ping to its own gateway are blocked, while PC1 opens http://www.branch.test. Press Check results, then read `show access-lists`.
courses.expected: PC1 and PC2 hold leases from .21 upward. PC2 resolves www.branch.test but is blocked from http://192.168.30.10, while PC1 opens http://www.branch.test. Both reach 198.51.100.10, and `show ip nat translations` shows their echoes translated to 203.0.113.2 (the first keeps ICMP ID 1, the second becomes 1024) plus the static 203.0.113.10 to 192.168.30.10 entry. PC3's pings to 203.0.113.10 are answered.

challenge.task: Static NAT exposes every service on Server1. Add an inbound list on R1 g0/1 that permits only web traffic to 203.0.113.10, drops everything else sent to that address, and lets all other packets through so that PAT keeps working. Then explain why a stateful firewall is the usual tool at a real Internet edge.

You explain that the list is stateless, matches the public address because inbound filtering runs before translation, and that a stateful firewall tracks sessions instead

questions.prompt: Why can a host with 192.168.10.21 not browse the Internet without NAT?

options.text: Private addresses cannot carry TCP sessions to servers that use public addresses
The Internet does not route RFC 1918 addresses, so replies could not come back
Web browsers refuse to open pages when the source address is a private one

questions.explanation: Many organizations use the same private ranges, so Internet routers carry no routes for them. NAT gives the traffic a public source address that replies can reach.

questions.prompt: Which kind of NAT lets Internet hosts start connections to an inside server?

options.text: Static NAT, a permanent one-to-one mapping
PAT on the users' outside interface
None: NAT blocks every inbound connection

questions.explanation: A static mapping exists before any traffic flows, so the router can translate a connection that starts outside. PAT entries only exist for sessions that inside hosts started.

questions.prompt: Two inside hosts both ping 198.51.100.10 with ICMP ID 1 through PAT on 203.0.113.2. What does the translation table show?

options.text: One shared entry for both hosts, since both of them used ICMP ID 1
Two entries on 203.0.113.2 with different IDs, such as 1 and 1024
Two entries, each with its own public address from the provider

questions.explanation: Each session needs a unique public address and port (or ID) pair, so the router renumbers the second host's ID. Replies can then be told apart.

questions.prompt: Hosts in 192.168.20.0/24 cannot reach the Internet, while 192.168.10.0/24 can. PAT uses `access-list 1`. What do you check first?

options.text: Whether access-list 1 permits 192.168.20.0 0.0.0.255
Whether VLAN 20 has the same name on S1 and R1
Whether the DNS server has records for the Internet

questions.explanation: Only sources that match the NAT access list are translated. Untranslated private sources cannot get replies from the Internet.

questions.prompt: A branch publishes its web server with static NAT and has no filter on the outside interface. Which statement is true?

options.text: Only web traffic reaches the server, because NAT acts as a simple firewall
The server stays hidden, because NAT always hides the inside addresses
Anything the server answers is reachable from the Internet until you filter it

questions.explanation: A one-to-one mapping forwards everything for the public address. Exposure is limited by filtering and by keeping the server's software secure, not by NAT.
